safety_line: Skin secretions can irritate eyes, nose, and airways, especially for people with asthma, and can bother pets that mouth one. Wash hands after contact; see a doctor if irritation doesn’t clear up.

traits: Large warty treefrog, up to about 5 inches — the largest treefrog in the US
Oversized toe pads compared to native treefrogs
Common around porch lights at night hunting insects
Grayish, brownish, or greenish with variable blotching, and rough, warty skin

look_alikes.difference: Cuban treefrogs are much larger with warty skin and oversized toe pads; green treefrogs are smaller, smooth-skinned, and usually have a white side stripe.
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, zoom in on the toe pads and overall size.

look_alikes.difference: Cuban treefrog is much larger (to 5.5 in) with bumpy skin and huge bulging eyes; squirrel treefrog stays under 1.5 in with smooth skin and small eyes.
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, zoom in on the eyes (bulging vs. normal) and skin texture (bumpy vs. smooth).

copy.what_it_means: An invasive species that eats Florida's smaller native treefrogs — one reason a porch chorus may have gone quiet. Wash hands after contact, and turning porch lights off (or switching to amber) removes the insect buffet that draws them in.
copy.fact: An invasive that eats Florida’s smaller native treefrogs — one reason your porch chorus may have gone quiet.
copy.blurb: Wash hands after contact. Turning porch lights off (or amber) removes the insect buffet that draws them.

tech_notes: Confirm size + toe pad size vs. native treefrogs. Humane removal/exclusion; avoid bare-hand contact due to skin secretions.

traits: Very large toad, often 4 to 6 inches or more, dry warty skin in gray, brown, olive or reddish-brown
Large, triangular parotoid glands bulge behind each eye, bigger than on any native toad
Bony ridges run from above the eyes down toward the snout
Found around outdoor lights, pet food bowls, pools and mulch beds at night, especially after rain

look_alikes.difference: Cane toad's glands behind the eyes are much larger, often as big as the eye; southern toad has smaller glands and bony head knobs it lacks
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, zoom in from above on the head and the size of the glands just behind the eyes; never handle it.

safety_line: A stronger skin irritant than a native toad's, and toxic to pets; if a pet mouths one, wipe its mouth/gums with a cloth (rinse only with the head tilted down) and call your vet right away.

copy.what_it_means: An invasive toad whose main real danger is to curious pets, not people. If dogs or cats have access to the yard at night, especially around a pool or food bowls left outside, it's worth knowing this one on sight and keeping pets from mouthing it.
copy.fact: It was originally brought to parts of the world, including nearby islands, to control agricultural pests, but it spread far beyond that job and became a problem itself.

tech_notes: Confirm large triangular parotoid glands vs. native southern toad before advising removal; safe handling is with gloves, and disposal per local wildlife guidance rather than general pest treatment.

review.notes: Verdict set to 'watch' rather than 'call' since most encounters don't involve pet contact and there's no Waves pest treatment for this species; urgency set to 'high' to reflect how serious the small number of pet-poisoning cases can be. traits: Smaller toad, usually under 3.5 inches, brick-red to gray, brown or black with warty skin
Distinct bony knobs and ridges on top of the head, between and behind the eyes
Parotoid glands behind the eyes are present but noticeably smaller than a cane toad's
Found in sandy soil, garden beds, and around lights at night

look_alikes.difference: Southern toad has smaller glands and distinct bony head knobs; cane toad's parotoid glands are much larger, often as big as the eye itself
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, zoom in from above on the head and the size of the glands just behind the eyes; never handle it.

safety_line: Its skin secretion can irritate a pet's mouth, far less than a cane toad's. Wipe the gums, rinse with the head tilted down so it doesn't swallow water, and call your vet if it persists.

copy.what_it_means: A native insect-eater that's become harder to find in areas where the invasive cane toad has moved in. It's harmless to leave alone, and worth telling apart from the cane toad since the two are treated very differently.
copy.fact: It digs backward into loose soil using its hind feet to bury itself during the day, re-emerging at night to feed.

tech_notes: No treatment indicated; confirm smaller parotoid glands and bony head knobs to distinguish from cane toad, since the two get very different guidance.

review.notes: Cane-toad-competition claim confirmed directly this session: UF/IFAS EDIS WEC387/UW432, "The Cane or 'Bufo' Toad (Rhinella marina) in Florida," states "people have noticed that native southern toads disappear or become uncommon in their neighborhoods when cane toads arrive," while noting the exact mechanism (competition, predation, or another factor) isn't settled. Range 'occasional' is consistent with this source; exact current SWFL county-level density still isn't separately quantified anywhere, but the qualitative scarcity claim is resolved. Owner approved 2026-09-27 (all fact-check-clean entries, after #5106); that decision completes any re-review this note describes as pending.

traits: Slim, smooth-skinned frog 1.25 to 2.5 inches long, usually bright green with a bold white to cream stripe along each side
Sometimes has small gold or white flecks scattered on its back
Sticky toe pads let it cling to glass doors, screens, and smooth plant leaves
Calls with a loud, repeated 'quonk-quonk' from vegetation near water on warm, humid nights

look_alikes.difference: Green treefrog is consistently bright green with a bold, complete white stripe; squirrel treefrog is smaller and more variable with a fainter stripe

look_alikes.difference: Cuban treefrog is much larger (to 5.5 in), bumpy-skinned with huge bulging eyes; green treefrog stays under 2.5 in, smooth-skinned, with a bold white stripe.

copy.what_it_means: A harmless, helpful little insect-eater that's a normal part of a Florida evening, not a pest. Clinging to a window or screen at night is exactly where it's supposed to be, hunting bugs drawn to the light.
copy.fact: Its toe pads work like tiny suction cups, letting it climb straight up glass doors and windows with ease.

tech_notes: No treatment indicated; beneficial insect predator, safe to relocate by hand if found somewhere inconvenient.

copy.what_it_means: A small, harmless, color-changing frog that shows up around porch lights and potted plants hunting insects. It's one of the most common backyard frogs here and never needs any kind of treatment.
